Text: $INTC $NBIS $ORCL $PLTR Let’s be clear about what happened. The earlier $70B figure was created by “grossing up” OpenAI’s revenue to make an apples-to-apples comparison with Anthropic, which counts the full value of sales made through cloud partners and records the partners’ share as an expense. OpenAI normally reports only its own net share, producing the $50B figure. Nothing suddenly disappeared. No $20B revenue collapse occurred. Yet the same accounting difference was repackaged as “OpenAI revenue is $20B lower than previously signaled,” triggering a massive selloff in $ORCL and other AI stocks. That framing was plainly misleading to the public and investors. Author: KavaStocks
Text: $SPCX $APLD $NBIS SpaceX reported tonight, and for a rocket company, they spent a lot of the call talking about power. Anyone holding the AI data center names, landlords and GPU clouds alike, had reason to listen. Musk said hyperscalers and smaller firms are hounding them for capacity, with enough demand to rent out their compute several times over. Renewals are coming in at higher rates, and the CFO said new deployments pay for themselves in under a year at those prices. That is what a seller's market sounds like. They are now targeting roughly 13 gigawatts by the end of next year, well above the range they gave a few weeks ago. Musk's timelines run on Elon time, and even after a healthy haircut that is a lot of turbines. Turbines happen to be the bottleneck he named, all the way down to casting the blades and vanes. A company that builds its own rocket engines is stuck in the same equipment line as everyone else trying to energize a data center. That is the whole argument for this group, said out loud by the most aggressive builder in the business. Capacity that is already powered and running is the scarce thing, and the people who have it get to choose their customers. Where they all part ways is how they get paid. SpaceX builds its own capacity, power plants included, and rents out the compute on short terms at spot prices. It collects every bit of the upside while the shortage lasts and reprices first if it ever ends. GPU clouds like Nebius also own the chips and sell the compute, mostly through multi-year contracts with some sold on demand. Landlords like Applied Digital lease the building and the power for years, and the tenant brings the GPUs. Rising compute prices reach the GPU clouds directly, through renewals and the hours they sell on demand. For the landlords, better compute economics put more cash behind the rent, and scarce energized power strengthens their hand on the next lease. They are three ways to own the same shortage, and tonight was good for all three. That is plenty of good news for a group the market spent last week treating like a crime scene. Every fear behind that selloff was about money. People worried about too much debt, too many neoclouds for the world to keep, bond yields that look like hazard pay, and a growing suspicion that half the financing in this industry is the industry lending to itself. SpaceX is in that club too, since part of its plan relies on funding partnerships with its own vendors and customers. Tonight's call was about the other side of the ledger, with more customers than compute, prices going up, and a turbine line nobody gets to skip. The two stories connect, and that is the part the market keeps missing. Expensive money slows new construction first, and slower construction stretches out the shortage SpaceX just described. That makes capacity that already exists worth more, whether it is a powered building or a cluster that is already racked and running. Tight money still bites, and it bites hardest on whoever carries the chips and the debt. The landlords mostly feel it through their tenants, which is why the name on the lease matters as much as the megawatts. It is a real risk to this buildout and a strange reason to sell the people who already have the capacity. If you did that last week, tonight was an uncomfortable call to sit through.

Text: $NBIS $IREN The market’s schizophrenia and persistent inconsistencies are particularly evident in the way neoclouds are currently being valued. The business model of these companies is built around a very simple principle: invest massively today in infrastructure to capture the structural explosion in compute demand tomorrow. It is therefore fundamentally contradictory to expect these companies to capture exponential growth while simultaneously penalizing them for the very investments required to build the capacity that will make that growth possible. Every major infrastructure revolution has been extraordinarily capital-intensive in its early stages: railroads in the 19th century, power grids, telecommunications and fiber networks, and later cloud infrastructure. AI is now triggering a new infrastructure cycle — potentially one of the largest technological and industrial investment waves we have ever witnessed. The fundamental question is therefore not simply: “How much are they spending today?” The real question is: “What economic returns will these assets generate once deployed, scaled and fully monetized?” That is where the winners and losers will ultimately be determined. Against this backdrop, the extreme volatility currently affecting some publicly traded neoclouds increasingly appears to reflect short-term positioning, flows and trading dynamics rather than any proportional deterioration in their long-term fundamentals. The market is looking at CAPEX. Long-term investors are looking at what that CAPEX is building. #ThoseWhoKnowKnow
